transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2026-11-03
Time: 14:00 UTC
Duration: 45 minutes
Attendees: Sofia Patel (Redwood AE), Ethan Chen (Redwood SE), Maya Reyes (BlueHarbor Head of Platform), Liam O'Connor (BlueHarbor SRE), Priya Kaur (BlueHarbor ML Eng)

Summary: Quick sync on this week's latency tuning work — saw TTFT improvements with new kernel + streaming flags; still probing sequence-length tail and batching effects. Agreed next steps to run a 1k request streaming benchmark and share kernel comparison spreadsheet.

Topics: TTFT numbers, streaming vs blocking, sequence length distribution, kernel choices (cutlass/fused attention/amoeba), KV cache behavior, quantization tradeoffs, next steps for canary

Transcript:
[00:00] Sofia (Redwood): Hey everyone, thanks for joining. Quick check in — same agenda as last week: results, any surprises, and next steps for the pilot.
[00:18] Maya (BlueHarbor): Yeah thanks. We pushed Ethan's kernel change to staging last night and ran some spot tests.
[00:27] Ethan (Redwood): Cool, sounds good — quick caveat, the change was the fused-attn patch + switching to the new cuda cutlass path for matmuls, so expect differences across sequence lengths.
[00:40] Priya (BlueHarbor): Initial numbers — TTFT median dropped from ~420ms to ~220ms for 256-token workloads, but p95 still around 780ms, so tail's stubborn.
[00:55] Liam (BlueHarbor): Also saw CPU spikes on the proxy side when streaming was off, we had to increase worker threads.
[01:12] Sofia: Okay that aligns with what we saw in our internal runs. Streaming tends to cut perceived TTFT since tokens come incrementally, but cold-start setup time can still dominate if KV cache misses or model loads occur.
[01:30] Priya: We did one run with streaming enabled and saw the first token come faster, but the total time to end-of-sequence was similar — curious if batching is interfering.
[01:46] Ethan: Right, if you're using continuous batching on the Redwood side, small streams can get batched which might add a micro-queue. We can tune the low-latency threshold so that streaming requests are prioritized.
[02:05] Maya: Can you explain the low-latency threshold? I thought batching was automatic.
[02:12] Ethan: Sure— there's a config knob that says: if request is flagged streaming or TTFT-priority, skip the normal batch window and route to a fast lane. But it's a tradeoff: throughput drops a bit.
[02:30] Liam: For BlueHarbor, throughput is less critical for auth flows where we need <300ms 95th. But we do have high TPS for background scoring where throughput matters.
[02:45] Sofia: Good to call that out — we can propose separate routes: auth route with tight latency SLO and a scoring route with batched throughput optimizations.
[03:02] Priya: Back to kernels — which one is the default you flipped? cutlass or the legacy path?
[03:10] Ethan: Default was legacy cuBLAS-ish code; we enabled the cutlass matmul path plus a fused attention kernel for that model. Also tested 4-bit quantization on the same run.
[03:26] Priya: Did quantization change the p95?
[03:31] Ethan: Mixed — quant reduced CPU/GPU memory and gave small steady improvements on median, but p95 still driven by long sequences and occasional kernel fallback when the fused kernel can't handle a shape, so it falls back to slower path.
[03:50] Maya: That fallback sounds bad. How often does it happen?
[03:55] Ethan: In our staging sample it was about 3-5% of requests at sequence lengths over 512 where attention breaks into a different codepath. We think kernel selector needs extra heuristics.
[04:12] Liam: We have a tail of longer conversations — about 8% of requests exceed 512 tokens during fraud investigations. So that matches.
[04:25] Sofia: So action items: we should either 1) adjust kernel selector to prefer stable slower path for long sequences, or 2) add a route that pins long-sequence requests to a dedicated variant. Thoughts?
[04:40] Priya: I like route pinning — it avoids impacting auth latency. But cost will go up.
[04:47] Maya: Cost is acceptable if we keep the auth route tight. For the fraud batch jobs, we can accept higher latency.
[04:55] Ethan: We can also try progressive streaming where we sample early tokens with fused kernels and then switch to the fallback for longer context. It's a bit complex but doable.
[05:12] Liam: About the CPU spikes — those look like proxy serialization issues when we have many streaming sessions open. Any recommendations?
[05:20] Ethan: Two short-term fixes: increase worker threads (what you did) and reduce chunk size so the proxy writes smaller frames; longer term we have an optimized streaming proxy in our dedicated runtime that has less serialization overhead.
[05:38] Priya: Do we have numbers for first token latency vs full end-to-end? We want TTFT specifically for user-facing auth.
[05:46] Sofia: Yes — from the runs you sent, first-token median is ~75ms with streaming enabled; full E2E median is ~220ms. That explains perceived responsiveness vs p95 tail.
[06:02] Maya: Great. For our SLOs we need p95 < 300ms for auth. We're close but not consistent yet.
[06:10] Ethan: Next tweak I recommend is lowering the streaming priority timeout to 5ms so that streaming requests don't sit in batching windows longer than that. That shrank median by ~30ms in our internal tests.
[06:26] Priya: Can you share the config you used?
[06:29] Ethan: I'll drop the exact config into the kernel spreadsheet — low_latency_threshold: 5ms, streaming_chunk_size: 64 tokens, batch_window: 20ms for regular routes.
[06:44] Maya: Perfect. Also saw some transcription oddities in logs where model name got truncated — minor but want consistent naming for auditing.
[06:52] Sofia: Noted — we'll use full model ids in the next runs.
[06:58] Liam: Any security/compliance notes? We're still waiting for the SOC2 appendix on streaming.
[07:05] Sofia: We shared the streaming security appendix last week; I'll re-share with an emphasis on encryption in transit and access logs.
[07:12] Maya: Thanks. Back to performance — Priya, do you have the sequence length distribution?
[07:18] Priya: Yes, I uploaded a CSV: median 120 tokens, 90th 420, 99th 980. Those long tails are from in-depth fraud case transcripts.
[07:30] Ethan: That distribution explains why p95 sits high — many ops fall into the fallback kernel region where fused kernels don't apply.
[07:38] Sofia: Two-pronged approach: kernel selector heuristics + routing long sequences to a dedicated variant. We should simulate cost delta for pinning.
[07:48] Maya: Can you give a rough cost estimate for a dedicated long-seq pool?
[07:53] Sofia: Off the top, a small dedicated pool handling 10% of traffic would add around 15-25% to GPU spend for that service, but would improve auth p95 by isolating it. I'll get a precise number after Ethan shares kernel perf numbers.
[08:08] Priya: On the topic of quantization — we saw occasional hallucinations when we forced 4-bit at high temperature. Not huge but a concern for accuracy-sensitive flows.
[08:20] Ethan: That's expected. For auth, low-temp generation is fine; for assistant-style flows we'd keep higher precision. We can set per-route quant profiles.
[08:31] Liam: One operational question — how do rollouts work if you change kernels? Can we A/B?
[08:37] Sofia: Yes we support canaries and A/B by route and model variant. You can do traffic splits and automatic rollback on regression signals.
[08:46] Maya: Priya, after your 1k streaming run, can you indicate if we need a canary?
[08:52] Priya: Will do. I'll include telemetry for first token, median, p95, and error rates.
[08:59] Ethan: Also include kernel selector logs so we can see fallback frequency.
[09:04] Priya: Yep.
[09:06] Maya: Any other surprises from last week's tests?
[09:10] Liam: We found one edge case where the KV cache keying failed when user IDs contained special chars — caused some cache misses and re-computation. Fixed in staging.
[09:22] Sofia: Good catch. We'll add a sanitizer to the client library.
[09:28] Priya: For the benchmarks, do you want microbenchmarks (single-model runs) or end-to-end?
[09:34] Ethan: Both — microbenchmarks let us isolate kernel perf; end-to-end shows real world including proxy and batching effects.
[09:41] Maya: Timeline wise we want to decide on canary by mid-November if numbers look good.
[09:48] Sofia: Sounds reasonable. We'll aim for shared artifacts by Thursday.
[09:53] Ethan: I'll have the kernel comparison CSV and notes up by 2026-11-05. The spreadsheet will include median/p95/p99 per kernel per seq length bucket.
[10:06] Priya: I'll run the 1k streaming test by 2026-11-10 and upload logs.
[10:13] Liam: I'll pull staging CPU/GPU utilization and forward.
[10:17] Maya: One last product question — can Redwood do dynamic quantization per-example?
[10:22] Ethan: We have per-route quantization; per-example is more experimental because it complicates caching. We can discuss but cautious.
[10:31] Priya: Understood.
[10:33] Sofia: Okay let's recap next steps...
[10:36] Sofia: Action items — Ethan share kernel spreadsheet; Priya run 1k streaming benchmark and upload logs; Liam share infra graphs. Redwood will re-share SOC2 appendix and streaming security note.
[10:47] Maya: Sounds good. Thanks everyone.
[10:50] Sofia: Thanks, we'll follow up in email.
[44:30] (meeting end)

Notes: transcript contains typical speech disfluencies; some proper nouns in logs may be truncated in automated transcription. Shared artifacts referenced: kernel-comparison.csv (link in CRM), streaming-security-appendix.pdf (link in shared drive), bench-results/2026-11-03-stream-1k.log (upload awaited).
